extracted.intended_audience: Catholic laypeople preparing for confession (penitents) and confessors
extracted.subtask_description: Practical catechetical guidance on preparing for and making the Sacrament of Penance (Confession): how to examine conscience, what sorrow/contrition is required, how to confess, and related behaviors and obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements to receive the Sacrament of Penance worthily
rubrics_metrics.description: To receive the Sacrament of Penance worthily we must do five things: (1) examine our conscience, (2) have sorrow for our sins, (3) make a firm resolution never more to offend God, (4) confess our sins to the priest, (5) accept the penance which the priest gives us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing: pray to the Holy Ghost for light and sorrow; examine by the Ten Commandments, Church precepts, capital sins, and duties of your state; contrition must be present (not merely the verbal act) before absolution; make a firm purpose of amendment and accept/perform the priest's penance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of conscience (general method)
rubrics_metrics.description: The examination of conscience is an earnest effort to recall to mind all the sins we have committed since our last worthy confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good examination calls to memory the Commandments of God, the precepts of the Church, the seven capital sins, and particular duties of one's state in life. Begin by asking how long since your last good confession and whether it was properly made; use the Commandments as a checklist to find concrete examples. Pray before beginning for light and grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine conscience using the Ten Commandments (concrete prompts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use each of the Ten Commandments as specific prompts (e.g., 'Have I honored God?', 'Have I taken the name of the Lord in vain?', 'Have I neglected Mass?').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each Commandment the text supplies sample questions and particular examples to recall sins (e.g., for 'Thou shalt not steal': restitution, cheating, failure to pay debts; for 'Thou shalt not kill': anger, revenge, giving scandal). These examples are given to help determine kinds, frequency, and circumstances of sins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine conscience on the precepts of the Church
rubrics_metrics.description: After the Commandments, examine yourself on the Church's precepts (e.g., hear Mass on Sundays/holy days, fast/abstain on prescribed days, confess at least once a year, receive Eucharist during Easter time, contribute to support pastors, marriage regulations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the precepts to ask specific questions (e.g., did I knowingly eat meat on Ash Wednesday?). The precepts may overlap with Commandment-based items (e.g., Mass attendance) but are separate checks on ecclesial obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine conscience on the seven capital sins and duties of state
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the capital sins—pride, gluttony, sloth, etc.—and consider duties specific to your state in life (school, work, family obligations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives concrete prompts: pride (vanity, disdain for the poor), gluttony (excess drinking), sloth (neglect of duty), and asks about fidelity in school/work (studying, honesty with employers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of proper contrition (interior, supernatural, universal, sovereign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sorrow (contrition) for sin should be interior (from the heart), supernatural (prompted by God's grace and motives of faith), universal (for all mortal sins without exception), and sovereign (grieve more for offending God than for any other misfortune).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interior: not mere outward display or tears; God sees the heart. Supernatural: sorrow must be because sin offends God (perfect contrition is sorrow from love of God; imperfect contrition is sorrow from fear of punishment). Universal: being sorry for all mortal sins is required since a single unrepented mortal sin blocks grace. Sovereign: one must prefer sorrow for offending God above other losses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfect vs. imperfect contrition and their sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of contrition: perfect contrition (sorrow because sin offends God) and imperfect contrition (attrition, sorrow because of fear of punishment or loss of Heaven).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perfect contrition is required to obtain forgiveness outside sacramental confession (e.g., in danger of death without access to a priest). Imperfect contrition, together with the priest's absolution, suffices for a worthy confession. Strive for perfect contrition but imperfect is acceptable when combined with sacramental absolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firm purpose of amendment and avoidance of near occasions of sin
rubrics_metrics.description: A firm purpose of sinning no more means a fixed resolve not only to avoid mortal sin but also its near occasions; one must resolve to avoid persons, places, and things that readily lead to sin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes voluntary vs. necessary occasions and near vs. remote occasions: avoid near occasions (where one 'usually falls into sin') such as bad companions, saloons, bad books, etc. Practical example: stop the leaking pipe (cause) before repairing plaster (effect). If one fears falling, that fear does not destroy contrition as long as one truly intends amendment and will use God's grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession defined and authorized forms (to a duly authorized priest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confession is the telling of our sins to a duly authorized priest for the purpose of obtaining forgiveness. 'Duly authorized' means a priest sent by the diocesan bishop in that diocese.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If speech is lost, one may write sins and give the paper to the priest (then destroy it); if memory poor, write and read sins in the confessional (then destroy); if language is not understood or penitent cannot speak, use signs and show sorrow; priest may adapt as with the speechless. Destroy written lists after confession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sins to confess: obligation and recommended practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Obliged to confess all mortal sins; it is commendable to confess venial sins as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you committed a venial sin after confession it does not necessarily bar Holy Communion (Eucharist will wipe out venial sins), but a mortal sin after confession does. The Church precept 'to confess at least once a year' is noted; frequency beyond that depends on conscience and need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief qualities of a good confession: humble, sincere, entire
rubrics_metrics.description: A good confession must be humble, sincere, and entire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humble: accuse oneself with deep shame and sorrow. Sincere: tell sins honestly and truthfully, neither exaggerating nor excusing. Entire: tell the number, kinds, and circumstances which change the nature of the sins (only circumstances that alter the gravity need be given).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to tell sins in confession (practical rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical rules for stating sins: tell only the sins (not long stories), do not mention names of others, be brief, give approximate numbers if exact count is unknown, tell your worst sin first, and if ashamed say so so the priest can help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not multiply counts by days (avoid overly detailed enumeration); avoid words like 'sometimes' or 'maybe'—give approximate numbers or frequency (e.g., times per day). If you cannot express exact words of an offense (cursing), simply say 'I cursed so many times.' If you are deaf, wait until others are heard or ask to be heard elsewhere. Speak loud enough to be heard but not too loud. If you forget a mortal sin without fault, it is forgiven; if you remember it later the same day, mention it then.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances that change a sin's nature must be confessed
rubrics_metrics.description: In confessing, one must state any circumstances that materially change the nature or gravity of the sin (e.g., stealing from a church, stealing so as to cause a person to starve).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not give unnecessary particulars that confuse or waste time; only report circumstances that make the sin sacrilegious or significantly worse or lesser in character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior and disposition while waiting for and entering confession
rubrics_metrics.description: While waiting: pray for pardon and sorrow; do not quarrel, cheat for place in line, or create confusion; do not keep the priest waiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gossip or noise which distracts others and the priest; if in mortal sin you should go that day regardless of inconvenience; if in a hurry ask permission to go first—do not force place unfairly; entering the confessional: bless yourself, begin with 'Bless me, father, for I have sinned' and state the time since last confession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance and performance of penance and the act of contrition
rubrics_metrics.description: Listen attentively to the penance the priest gives, say the act of contrition while he pronounces absolution, and do not leave the confessional until dismissed; perform the penance as soon as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the priest does not specify when to perform the penance, do it as soon as you can. The penance is part of satisfaction; leaving before the priest dismisses is forbidden. Penance should be done promptly to complete the sacramental act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willful concealment of mortal sin invalidates confession and is sacrilegious
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a grievous offense willfully to conceal a mortal sin in confession because one thereby tells a lie to the Holy Ghost and makes the confession worthless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealing a mortal sin is likened to denying the truth before God and increases guilt (sacrilege). The penitent must not be ashamed to confess sins; the shame itself can be part of penance. If a sin was willfully concealed, special steps (see further canon/catechetical instruction beyond this chunk) are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling forgotten mortal sins
rubrics_metrics.description: If without your fault you forget to confess a mortal sin, your confession is still worthy and the sin is forgiven; but if you recall it later you must tell it in your next confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intentionally tried to forget, the confession is invalid. If you remember the forgotten sin the same day or while still in church, it is included and forgiven; otherwise, mention it next time you confess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priests exercise the power to forgive by hearing confession and granting pardon
rubrics_metrics.description: The priests of the Church exercise the power of forgiving sins by hearing the confession of sins and granting pardon for them as ministers of God and in His name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many sins are secret, confession is necessary for priests to know what to remit; priests act as ministers exercising the power given by Christ ('Whose sins you shall forgive...'). This is the theological/authority basis for the sacrament and for the penitent's obligation to confess to a priest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case provisions for communication or incapacity
rubrics_metrics.description: If the penitent cannot speak or write, or the priest does not understand the language, alternative methods (writing, signs) may be used to make a valid confession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you write your sins on paper to read in confession, destroy the paper afterward; if dying and language unknown, indicate sorrow by signs and show repentance; the priest will accommodate and act as he would with the speechless. Ensure privacy and destruction of notes to maintain confidentiality.
